definitions.definition: A mapping between two systems that shows they have the same structure or pattern, even if they look different on the surface.
definitions.example: A map of a subway system is isomorphic to the actual subway lines because the connections between stations match up, even though the map is not the same as the real tracks.

definitions.definition: Money that a government declares to be legal tender, but which is not backed by a physical commodity like gold or silver.
definitions.example: The US dollar today is fiat currency because it is not redeemable for gold, unlike dollars before 1971.

definitions.definition: Energy that appears to come from nowhere, violating the law of conservation of energy; in this framework, it refers to money created without corresponding real value.
definitions.example: Printing money without producing goods is like adding phantom energy to a system, which causes waste heat (inflation) instead of useful work.

definitions.definition: A statement or principle that is accepted as true without proof, serving as a starting point for further reasoning.
definitions.example: In geometry, 'through any two points there is exactly one line' is an axiom.

definitions.definition: A fundamental law of physics stating that energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transformed from one form to another.
definitions.example: When you burn gasoline in a car, the chemical energy is converted into heat and motion, but the total amount of energy stays the same.

definitions.definition: A claim that a system violates the laws of thermodynamics, specifically by creating something from nothing, which is impossible in physics but applied here to economics.
definitions.example: Creating money out of thin air is called thermodynamic fraud because it mimics a perpetual motion machine, which is impossible in physics.

definitions.definition: Based on observation or experience rather than theory or logic alone.
definitions.example: A doctor tests a new drug empirically by giving it to patients and seeing if they get better.

definitions.definition: A way of showing how the parts of one system correspond to the parts of another system, revealing a shared pattern or structure.
definitions.example: Comparing the way blood flows through veins to the way water flows through pipes is a structural mapping.

definitions.definition: A state of increasing randomness or chaos throughout an entire system, often measured as entropy.
definitions.example: If you stop organizing your room, it will naturally become more messy over time—that's systemic disorder.

definitions.definition: The confidence that people have in an organization or system, such as a government or bank, to act reliably and honestly.
definitions.example: People deposit money in a bank because they have institutional trust that the bank will keep it safe.

definitions.definition: The nature of a thing's existence or reality—whether it is a fundamental law of the universe or a human-made rule.
definitions.example: The law of gravity has a different ontological status than a traffic law: one is a fact of nature, the other is a human invention.

definitions.definition: Another name for the conservation of energy: energy cannot be created or destroyed, only changed in form.
definitions.example: When you eat food, your body converts the chemical energy into heat and movement, but the total energy is conserved.

definitions.definition: A monetary system where a country's currency is directly linked to a fixed amount of gold, and can be exchanged for gold.
definitions.example: Under the gold standard, you could take a dollar bill to a bank and get a specific amount of gold in return.

definitions.definition: A general increase in prices and fall in the purchasing value of money over time.
definitions.example: If a candy bar costs $1 today and $1.10 next year, that's inflation—your money buys less than before.

definitions.definition: A hypothetical machine that can operate indefinitely without an external energy source, violating the conservation of energy.
definitions.example: A wheel that spins forever without any power source is a perpetual motion machine, but it's impossible because friction always slows it down.

definitions.definition: A measure of disorder or randomness in a system; in thermodynamics, it always increases over time in a closed system.
definitions.example: An ice cube melting into a puddle increases entropy because the water molecules become more randomly arranged.

definitions.definition: A theoretical state where a system reaches maximum entropy, with no usable energy left to do work, often applied to the universe.
definitions.example: If you leave a hot cup of coffee in a cold room, eventually both will reach the same temperature and no more heat will flow—that's like a small-scale heat death.

definitions.definition: A change from one state of matter to another, like solid to liquid; used here metaphorically to describe a major shift in a system.
definitions.example: Water boiling into steam is a phase transition; the 1971 Nixon Shock is described as a phase transition in the monetary system.

definitions.definition: A quantity that only goes up or stays the same, never decreases.
definitions.example: Your age is monotonically increasing—you never get younger.

definitions.definition: The idea that the universe has a built-in moral order set by God, which is reflected in physical laws like conservation.
definitions.example: The belief that stealing is wrong because it violates a divine moral structure, not just because it's against the law.

definitions.definition: In this framework, a measure of how well a system aligns with its fundamental moral or physical principles; conservation of coherence means the system is consistent and stable.
definitions.example: A well-tuned engine runs smoothly because all parts work together—that's coherence; a sputtering engine loses coherence.

definitions.definition: The act of proving a statement or theory false by showing evidence that contradicts it.
definitions.example: If someone claims all swans are white, finding a black swan falsifies that claim.

definitions.definition: The study of how parts of a system are connected and arranged, ignoring specific sizes or shapes.
definitions.example: A donut and a coffee cup have the same topology because they both have one hole, even though they look different.

definitions.definition: The economic phenomenon where new money injected into an economy benefits those who receive it first (like banks) at the expense of those who receive it later (like workers).
definitions.example: If the government prints new money and gives it to banks first, bankers can buy goods before prices rise, while ordinary people face higher prices later.

definitions.definition: Reducing the value of a currency by lowering the amount of precious metal in coins or by printing more money without backing.
definitions.example: Ancient Romans debased their coins by mixing in cheaper metals, so the coins were worth less.

definitions.definition: The study of salvation, especially how people are saved from sin and its consequences according to religious beliefs.
definitions.example: In Christianity, soteriology explores how Jesus's death and resurrection save believers.
definitions.first_appearance: Not in text (but included as category example)

definitions.definition: The study of sin, its origins, and its effects on humanity and the world.
definitions.example: Hamartiology asks questions like 'What is sin?' and 'How does sin affect our relationship with God?'
definitions.first_appearance: Not in text (but included as category example)

definitions.definition: The process of becoming more holy or morally pure, often through divine grace or spiritual growth.
definitions.example: A person trying to become more patient and kind over time is undergoing sanctification.
definitions.first_appearance: Not in text (but included as category example)

definitions.definition: The act of making amends for a wrong or sin, often through a sacrifice or payment.
definitions.example: In Christianity, Jesus's death is seen as an atonement for the sins of humanity.
definitions.first_appearance: Not in text (but included as category example)

definitions.definition: A one-to-one matching between two sets where every element in one set is paired with exactly one element in the other set, and vice versa.
definitions.example: If you have three hats and three heads, putting one hat on each head is a bijection.
definitions.first_appearance: Not in text (but included as category example)

definitions.definition: Refers to Emmy Noether's theorem, which states that every conservation law (like conservation of energy) is linked to a symmetry in the universe.
definitions.example: Noether's theorem explains why energy is conserved: because the laws of physics don't change over time.
definitions.first_appearance: Not in text (but included as category example)

definitions.definition: A mathematical object that describes relationships between sets of numbers or vectors, often used in physics to represent things like stress or curvature.
definitions.example: A tensor can describe how a rubber band stretches in different directions when you pull it.
definitions.first_appearance: Not in text (but included as category example)

definitions.definition: The branch of philosophy that studies the nature of being, existence, and reality.
definitions.example: Ontology asks questions like 'Does God exist?' or 'What does it mean for something to be real?'
definitions.first_appearance: Not in text (but included as category example)

definitions.definition: The study of knowledge: how we know things, what counts as evidence, and the limits of what we can know.
definitions.example: Epistemology asks 'How do you know that the sun will rise tomorrow?'
definitions.first_appearance: Not in text (but included as category example)

definitions.definition: Something that depends on other conditions or could be different; not necessary or guaranteed.
definitions.example: Whether it rains tomorrow is contingent on the weather patterns, not a fixed fact.
definitions.first_appearance: Not in text (but included as category example)

definitions.definition: Something that must be true or exist, and cannot be otherwise.
definitions.example: In logic, 'all bachelors are unmarried' is a necessary truth because it's true by definition.
definitions.first_appearance: Not in text (but included as category example)

definitions.definition: A hypothetical field in the Theophysics framework that represents the moral or coherence structure of reality, analogous to a physical field.
definitions.example: The chi-field is like a moral gravity that pulls systems toward coherence and away from disorder.
definitions.first_appearance: Not in text (but included as category example)

definitions.definition: A mathematical function in the Theophysics framework that measures how coherent or aligned a system is with its fundamental principles.
definitions.example: The coherence functional is like a score that tells you how 'in tune' a system is with reality.
definitions.first_appearance: Not in text (but included as category example)

definitions.definition: A concept in the Theophysics framework describing how moral choices can 'bend' the structure of reality, similar to how mass bends spacetime in general relativity.
definitions.example: A lie might create moral curvature that distorts relationships and trust, like a heavy ball warping a rubber sheet.
definitions.first_appearance: Not in text (but included as category example)

definitions.definition: Based on observation or experience rather than theory or pure logic.
definitions.example: A scientist uses empirical data from experiments to test a hypothesis.

definitions.definition: Able to be proven false by evidence; a key requirement for a scientific theory.
definitions.example: The claim 'all planets orbit the sun' is falsifiable because we could find a planet that doesn't.

definitions.definition: A statement that has been proven to be true based on axioms and logical reasoning.
definitions.example: The Pythagorean theorem (a² + b² = c²) is a proven fact about right triangles.
definitions.first_appearance: Not in text (but included as category example)

definitions.definition: A mathematical shorthand for the conservation of energy: the change in total energy of a closed system is zero.
definitions.example: If you put 100 joules of energy into a system, you get 100 joules out (in some form), so ΔE = 0.

definitions.definition: Einstein's equation showing that energy (E) and mass (m) are equivalent, with the speed of light squared (c²) as the conversion factor.
definitions.example: A tiny amount of mass can be converted into a huge amount of energy, like in a nuclear reactor.

definitions.definition: An international monetary system established in 1944 that tied currencies to the US dollar, which was convertible to gold at a fixed rate.
definitions.example: Under Bretton Woods, countries agreed to keep their currencies stable relative to the dollar, which was backed by gold.

definitions.definition: The 1971 decision by President Nixon to end the direct convertibility of the US dollar to gold, effectively ending the Bretton Woods system.
definitions.example: The Nixon Shock meant that dollars could no longer be exchanged for gold, making them pure fiat currency.

definitions.definition: Separated or disconnected from something that was previously linked.
definitions.example: When the dollar was decoupled from gold, its value was no longer tied to a fixed amount of gold.

definitions.definition: The underlying material or foundation that supports something else.
definitions.example: Soil is the substrate for plants, providing nutrients and support.

definitions.definition: Investment in projects or assets that are not economically productive, often due to distorted signals like low interest rates from inflation.
definitions.example: Building too many luxury apartments when people need affordable housing is a malinvestment.

definitions.definition: The ability of a material to absorb and store heat energy, which can delay temperature changes.
definitions.example: A thick stone wall has high thermal mass, so it stays cool during the day and releases heat at night.

definitions.definition: A situation where falling prices lead to reduced spending, which causes further price drops and economic contraction.
definitions.example: If everyone expects prices to fall, they delay purchases, causing businesses to lower prices even more, creating a downward spiral.

definitions.definition: Inflexibility or inability to adapt to changing conditions.
definitions.example: A rigid monetary system might not allow enough money supply to grow with the economy, causing problems.

definitions.definition: The way the connections and structure of one system correspond to those of another system.
definitions.example: A subway map and the actual tracks have the same topology because the stations are connected in the same order.

definitions.definition: The process of a system reaching a state of balance, where all parts are at the same temperature or energy level.
definitions.example: When you put ice in a warm drink, the ice melts and the drink cools until both reach the same temperature—that's equilibration.

definitions.definition: The amount of goods or services that a unit of money can buy.
definitions.example: If a dollar buys less candy than it did last year, its purchasing power has decreased.

definitions.definition: A statistical measure of income or wealth inequality within a population, where 0 means perfect equality and 1 means maximum inequality.
definitions.example: A country with a Gini coefficient of 0.3 has more equal income distribution than one with 0.6.

definitions.definition: A point on a curve where the direction of change shifts, such as from increasing to decreasing.
definitions.example: If a company's profits were rising but then start falling, the peak is an inflection point.

definitions.definition: A figure of speech that describes one thing as if it were another, to suggest a comparison.
definitions.example: Saying 'time is a thief' is a metaphor because time doesn't literally steal, but it can feel like it takes things away.

definitions.definition: A comparison between two things that are similar in some way, often used to explain something unfamiliar.
definitions.example: Explaining how electricity flows through wires by comparing it to water flowing through pipes is an analogy.

definitions.definition: Lack of equality or balance between two sides or parts.
definitions.example: A seesaw with one heavy person and one light person has asymmetry—it tilts to one side.

definitions.definition: Consumer Price Index: a measure of the average change over time in the prices paid by consumers for goods and services.
definitions.example: If the CPI goes up by 2% in a year, that means the cost of living has increased by about 2%.

definitions.definition: A ratio comparing a country's total debt to its gross domestic product (total economic output), used to gauge financial health.
definitions.example: If a country has a debt-to-GDP ratio of 100%, its debt is equal to the value of everything it produces in a year.

definitions.definition: A situation where wages adjusted for inflation do not increase over time, meaning workers' purchasing power stays flat or declines.
definitions.example: If your salary stays the same for years but prices go up, you experience real wage stagnation.
